semantic-html.desc: Choose elements for their meaning: header, nav, main, article, section, aside, footer.
semantic-html.what:
Definition: Semantic HTML means choosing tags for what the content means, not how it looks. Use <nav> for navigation, <main> for the primary content, and <article> for a self-contained post.

Styling is CSS's job. A tag's job is to say what the element is.
semantic-html.analogy: Think of a book with chapters, headings, and an index. If it were one giant paragraph, nobody could find anything. Semantic tags are the book's index.
semantic-html.why: Screen readers, search engine crawlers, and reader mode all use the meaning of your tags to understand the page. A <button> gets keyboard activation (Enter/Space) and focus for free. A <div onclick> needs all of that added by hand, and it is often forgotten.
pros: Better accessibility and SEO with no extra work
The structure is obvious just from reading the tags
cons: Beginners often struggle to decide between <section> and <div>
gotchas: A <section> without a heading is almost always wrong. Use a <div> when you only need a styling hook
A page should have only one <main>
Don't skip heading levels (h1 → h4), and never pick a heading just for its size. Control size with CSS
terms: A tag whose name describes its purpose, such as <nav>, <main>, or <article>.
A major region of the page that screen reader users can jump to directly.
Wrapping everything in <div>, so browsers and assistive technology can't tell what anything is.
where: <article> plus a clean heading hierarchy works well for SEO and reader mode.
<main>, <nav>, and <button> give you keyboard and screen reader support almost for free.

html-doc-structure.q: Walk me through the essential contents of a <head>. Why does the viewport meta tag matter?</head>
html-doc-structure.qsub: What is the difference between placing a <script> in the head, at the end of the body, and using defer?</script>
html-doc-structure.what:
Definition: This is the skeleton of every HTML page: doctype, <html lang>, <head> (metadata, not visible), and <body> (visible content).

The <head> holds the charset, viewport, title, stylesheet links, and description.
html-doc-structure.why: Without a doctype, the browser falls back to quirks mode and older behavior, including the old box model. Without the viewport meta tag, mobile browsers render the page as a tiny zoomed-out desktop layout. The lang attribute lets screen readers pick the right pronunciation and helps translation tools.
cons: You have to remember the boilerplate (frameworks and templates usually handle it)
gotchas: Never use user-scalable=no. Blocking zoom is an accessibility problem
Declare the charset within the first 1024 bytes, or the browser may guess the encoding wrong
Put stylesheets in the and use defer on scripts. Otherwise rendering is blocked
terms: <!doctype html> tells the browser to use standards mode, not quirks mode.
Tells mobile browsers to lay out the page at the device width instead of a zoomed-out desktop width.
where: Every page needs this boilerplate, without exception.
Titles, descriptions, and Open Graph tags drive search results and social previews.

forms-inputs.qsub: What is the difference between GET and POST form submission?
forms-inputs.what:
Definition: A <form> collects user input and sends it to the server (action + method). Every field needs a name and a <label>.

Picking the right type brings up the right keyboard on mobile, and the browser runs basic validation for you.
forms-inputs.why: A placeholder is not a label. It disappears as soon as the user types and is unreliable for screen readers. Native forms give you submit-on-Enter, autofill, and password manager support for free. Custom div-based forms break all of that.
pros: Keyboard support, autofill, and submit-on-Enter for free
Better mobile UX with the right input type
cons: Customizing the native look can be difficult
gotchas: A <button> inside a form defaults to type submit. Give non-submit buttons type="button"
A field without a name is not sent on submit
Don’t use a placeholder as a substitute for a label
terms: Use <label for=id> or wrap the input in the label. Clicking the label focuses the input and screen readers announce its name.
The key of the field in the submitted data. Without a name, the value is never sent.
Types like email, number, and date give a suitable mobile keyboard and free validation.
where: Use type=email, type=password, and autocomplete so password managers work.
A GET form puts the state in the URL, so results are shareable and the back button works.

form-validation.what:
Definition: You can validate with HTML attributes alone: required, minlength, pattern, min/max, and type=email. The browser blocks submission and shows an error bubble.

From JavaScript you get form.checkValidity(), reportValidity(), and the input.validity object.
form-validation.why: For basic validation you rarely need a library. Client-side validation is only for UX. Always validate again on the server, because anyone can bypass the browser with DevTools.
pros: Accessible, localized error messages for free
cons: Error bubble styling is limited
Complex cross-field logic needs JavaScript
gotchas: Client validation is not a security measure. Re-validate on the server
:invalid shows red on page load. Use :user-invalid or a touched state instead
Adding novalidate turns off native validation
terms: The browser's built-in validation: required, pattern, min, max, and type-based checks.
A JavaScript API for setting a custom error message. An empty string clears the error.
A pseudo-class that matches the invalid state only after the user has interacted, not on page load.
where: Most fields are covered by required, pattern, and type.
Cross-field rules like “passwords must match” can use setCustomValidity.

media-elements.what:
Definition: Every <img> needs alt text and width/height, plus loading="lazy" when it is offscreen. Use srcset + sizes for responsive images and <picture> for different crops or formats.

For <video> and <audio>, add controls, set preload deliberately, and provide captions with <track>.
media-elements.why: Images are usually the heaviest part of a page, and sending a 2000 px image to a phone wastes bandwidth. Without width and height, the layout jumps when the image loads, which hurts CLS.
pros: The browser picks the best candidate automatically
cons: Writing correct sizes is tricky, and a wrong value makes the browser download a larger image than needed
gotchas: Don't use loading=lazy on the LCP (hero) image
Always set width/height or aspect-ratio, or the layout will shift
In alt text, don't write 'image of...'. Describe the image's purpose
terms: A text substitute for the image, read by screen readers and shown if the image fails. Use alt="" for decorative images.
Gives the browser several image sizes so it can pick the best one for the screen size and pixel density.
Art direction: serve different crops or formats (AVIF/WebP) on different screens.
where: loading=lazy keeps the initial load light.

a11y-aria.q: What is the first rule of ARIA? When should you reach for aria-* attributes?
a11y-aria.what:
Definition: The first route to accessibility is semantic HTML. Use ARIA only when no native element can do the job, such as custom tabs, comboboxes, or live updates (aria-live).

ARIA only changes what assistive technology is told. You still have to implement keyboard behavior and focus yourself.
a11y-aria.why: Bad ARIA is worse than no ARIA. If you add role="button" but don’t handle Enter and Space, a screen reader user hears a button that does nothing. Hence the rule: native first, ARIA last.
pros: Custom widgets become usable with assistive technology
Icon-only controls get an accessible name
cons: Misuse causes real problems, so you need to test with a screen reader
gotchas: Never put aria-hidden="true" on a focusable element
role adds no behavior. You must write the keyboard handling yourself
If there is a visible label, use aria-labelledby or
terms: Accessibility attributes (role, aria-*) that give assistive technology extra meaning.
If a native element exists, don't use ARIA: <button> beats div role=button.
When a modal or menu opens, move focus inside it. When it closes, return focus to where it was.
where: Trap focus, set aria-modal, and close on Esc. A native <dialog> is the best option.
aria-live announces changes to screen readers.
codeSwap: live region: dynamic status announce karta hai -->
icon-only button needs an accessible name -->

script-loading.q: What is the difference between async and defer? Which would you use for a third-party analytics script?
script-loading.qsub: Why can a <script> in the <head> hurt First Contentful Paint?</head></script>
script-loading.what:
Definition: A normal <script> pauses HTML parsing. defer downloads in parallel and runs after parsing finishes, in order. async runs as soon as it finishes downloading, with no order guarantee.

type="module" scripts behave like defer by default.
script-loading.why: If a script blocks the parser, the user stares at a blank screen and FCP/LCP suffer. With the right attribute, the HTML renders first and the JavaScript loads afterward.
cons: async scripts run in unpredictable order, which breaks dependencies
gotchas: Inline scripts are not affected by defer/async
Don't use async on scripts that depend on each other
defer scripts run before DOMContentLoaded
terms: The parser stops until the script is downloaded and executed, which delays rendering.
Downloads in parallel and runs in order after HTML parsing.
Downloads in parallel and runs as soon as it is ready, in no guaranteed order.
where: defer: runs in order once the DOM is ready.
async: the script doesn't depend on any other script.
codeSwap: independent third-party (analytics): order ki parwah nahi -->
app code: order matters, DOM ready ke baad -->
app code: order matters, runs after the DOM is ready -->

html-data-attrs.name: data-* Attributes & the DOM
html-data-attrs.qsub: When is a data attribute the wrong tool for holding state?
html-data-attrs.what:
Definition: data-* attributes store small pieces of custom data on an element. JavaScript reads them through dataset, and CSS can match them with attribute selectors ([data-state="open"]).

Values are always strings.
html-data-attrs.why: They are a simple way to connect server-rendered HTML to JavaScript, or to expose state to CSS. They are not a real state store, though. Keep application state in JavaScript or your framework.
pros: Context lives right in the markup, with no extra lookup
Usable from both CSS and JavaScript
cons: Values are strings, so they are a poor fit for large data
gotchas: Never store sensitive data in data-*. It is visible in the page source
data-user-id → dataset.userId (kebab-case becomes camelCase)
Screen readers don't read data-*. Use ARIA or semantic markup to convey meaning
terms: A custom attribute starting with data-, used to store small extra data in HTML.
The JavaScript API: el.dataset.userId reads the 'data-user-id' attribute in camelCase.
A stable way to find an element from JavaScript or tests, separate from styling.
where: With data-action, a single listener can handle many buttons.
Toggle styles with data-state or data-theme instead of extra classes.

selectors.name: Selectors & Combinators
selectors.desc: Type, class, id, and attribute selectors; descendant, child (>), and sibling (+, ~) combinators; :is() and :where().
selectors.q: Explain the different CSS combinators with examples. What does :where() add over :is()?
selectors.qsub: What is the difference between .a .b and .a > .b?
selectors.what:
Definition: A selector says which elements a rule applies to: type (p), class (.card), id (#nav), or attribute ([href^="https"]). Combinators let you target precisely by relationship.

:is() and :where() collapse repeated selectors into one.
selectors.why: The simpler and flatter the selector, the easier the CSS is to maintain. Long descendant chains (.a .b .c .d) are tied to the HTML structure, so when the markup changes, the styles break.
cons: Deep chains are fragile and raise specificity
gotchas: :is() takes the specificity of its most specific argument, while :where() always has zero
Avoid the universal * and overly deep selectors
~ matches only later siblings, never earlier ones
terms: The relationship between selectors: space (descendant), > (child), + (next sibling), ~ (later siblings).
They shorten selector lists. :where() adds zero specificity.
where: Flat class selectors (.card, .card__title) are the safest.
Structural rules like h2 + p and article > p suit prose content.

specificity.name: Specificity & the Cascade
specificity.desc: How the browser resolves conflicting rules: specificity (id > class > type), source order, and importance.
specificity.q: How is CSS specificity calculated? How would you resolve two rules fighting over the same element?
specificity.qsub: Where does !important sit in the cascade, and why is it a code smell?
specificity.what:
Definition: When two rules conflict on the same property, the browser checks importance first, then specificity (the count of IDs, classes, and types). If it is still a tie, the rule written later wins.

Think of specificity as a triple of (ids, classes, types). For example, #a .b p = (1,1,1).
specificity.why: Most “Why isn’t my style applying?” problems come down to specificity. To avoid specificity wars (an !important over another !important), use flat, low-specificity selectors and @layer.
cons: Specificity wars make CSS messy and brittle
gotchas: No number of chained classes beats an ID (classes always rank below IDs, so 11 classes never beat 1 ID)
An !important can only be overridden by another !important, so the chain keeps growing
An inline style can only be overridden by !important
terms: The weight of a selector: inline > id > class/attribute/pseudo-class > type/pseudo-element.
Origin and importance first, then specificity, then source order (later wins).
Overrides the normal cascade. It is hard to justify using it outside a deliberate override.
where: Low-specificity base styles that are easy to override.
Override library styles with @layer or a slightly more specific selector.
codeSwap: /* same specificity -> the later one wins */

inheritance.name: Inheritance & initial/inherit/unset
inheritance.desc: Which properties inherit (color, font) and which don't (margin, border); the inherit, initial, unset, and revert keywords.
inheritance.q: Which CSS properties inherit by default and which do not? How do you force inheritance?
inheritance.qsub: What is the difference between unset and revert?
inheritance.what:
Definition: Some properties, mostly text-related ones, are passed down to child elements automatically. Box-related properties are not.

Keywords: inherit (take the parent’s value), initial (the spec default), unset, and revert.
inheritance.why: This is why setting font-family once on the body styles the whole page. It is also why button and input look different: the browser gives them their own default font instead of inheriting, so you need to write font: inherit.
cons: You have to remember which properties inherit
gotchas: all: unset also removes display, so be careful
Inherited percentage and em values are passed down as computed values, not as the original expression
Custom properties (--x) inherit by default
terms: unset inherits if the property is inheritable and otherwise resets to initial. revert goes back to the browser default.
where: Set it on body to cover the whole site.

box-model.name: The Box Model & box-sizing
box-model.desc: Content, padding, border, and margin; content-box vs border-box; why border-box is the sane default.
box-model.q: Explain the CSS box model. What does box-sizing: border-box change and why do people set it globally?
box-model.qsub: A div has width:200px, padding:20px, border:5px. How wide is it in each box-sizing mode?
box-model.what:
Definition: Every element is a rectangle: content, then padding around it, then border, then margin (the outer space).

box-sizing: border-box makes width: 200px the width of the whole box, padding and border included.
box-model.why: With content-box, width:100%; padding:20px overflows the parent (100% + 40px). That's why almost every project applies a global border-box reset.
cons: Legacy or third-party CSS may assume content-box
gotchas: Margin sits outside the box, so the element's background does not paint it
width: 100% plus padding overflows in content-box
Vertical margin and padding on inline elements don't affect the layout
terms: Every element is a box with four layers: content → padding → border → margin.
The default: width applies to the content only, and padding and border are added on top.
width includes padding and border, so sizing is predictable.
where: Width and padding calculations stay simple.
codeSwap: /* total 300px, padding aur border ke saath */

display.name: Display: block / inline / inline-block
display.desc: How elements flow: block (full width), inline (no box dimensions), and inline-block (box dimensions plus inline flow).
display.q: What is the difference between block, inline, and inline-block? Give a use case for each.
display.qsub: Why can you not set width/height on a pure inline element?
display.what:
Definition: display decides how an element flows. div and p are block, span and a are inline, inline-block mixes both, and none removes the element from the layout entirely.

Today, flex and grid are the usual choice for layout.
display.why: Problems like “my span’s width isn’t working” or “a gap appears below an image” are solved by understanding the display model. The whitespace gap between inline-block elements comes from the same place.
pros: The foundation for flex and grid
cons: Quirks such as gaps between inline-block elements
gotchas: display:none also removes the element from the accessibility tree, but opacity:0 does not
width/height are ignored on inline elements
display:none elements can't be transitioned the usual way, because they have no box to animate
terms: Takes the full width and starts on a new line. Width, height, and margin all work.
Flows within text. Width and height are ignored, and vertical margins have no layout effect.
Flows like inline but accepts width and height like block.
where: display:block removes the gap below an image.
codeSwap: /* inline image ke neeche baseline gap hatata hai */
/* removes the baseline gap below an inline image */

margin-collapse.name: Margin Collapsing
margin-collapse.desc: Adjacent vertical margins collapse to the larger value; when it happens and how to prevent it.
margin-collapse.q: What is margin collapsing? Show a case where it surprises developers.
margin-collapse.qsub: How do you stop two vertical margins from collapsing?
margin-collapse.what:
Definition: When the vertical margins of block elements touch, they don't add up. The larger one wins (20px and 30px give 30px).

This happens only in the vertical direction, in normal block flow. Margins of flex and grid items do not collapse.
margin-collapse.why: It is intentional: spacing between paragraphs shouldn't double. The surprise comes when a child's margin-top pushes the parent down along with it.
pros: Avoids doubled spacing in vertical rhythm
cons: Surprising behavior when debugging layout
gotchas: Horizontal margins never collapse
Margins of flex items, grid items, and floats don't collapse
gap is a good way to avoid margin collapse
terms: Adjacent vertical margins don't add. The larger one remains.
Block Formatting Context. Child margins inside it don't collapse through its edges.
A child's top margin escapes through the parent when nothing (padding or border) separates them.
where: Use flow-root to prevent unwanted collapse.
codeSwap: /* child ka margin parent ke bahar leak hota hai */
/* the child's margin leaks outside the parent */

units.name: Units — px, em, rem, %, vw/vh, ch
units.desc: Absolute vs relative units; em (relative to font-size) vs rem (relative to the root); viewport and content units.
units.q: What is the difference between em and rem? When would you choose each?
units.qsub: Why can nested em values compound unexpectedly?
units.what:
Definition: Absolute: px. Relative: % (of the parent), em, rem, viewport units (vw, vh, dvh), and content units (ch, ex).

A common convention: rem for font sizes, em for spacing inside a component, and px for borders.
units.why: If the user raises the default font size in their browser, layouts built with rem scale accordingly, but px ones don't. That's a real accessibility win. ch gives you a text-width limit (for example max-width: 65ch) that keeps line length readable.
cons: Nested em values compound, which is confusing
gotchas: The html { font-size: 62.5% } trick can override user preferences
em refers to the parent’s font-size when used for font-size, but to the element’s own font-size for padding
100vh can be taller than the visible area on mobile because of the address bar
terms: Relative to the root (html) font-size. Predictable and best for accessibility.
Relative to the element’s own font-size (in padding/margin) or the parent’s (in font-size). Nesting causes compounding.
1% of the viewport width or height, and the width of the '0' character.
where: Use rem for sizes so user settings are respected.
em-based padding scales a component with its font-size.

css-variables.name: CSS Custom Properties (Variables)
css-variables.desc: --var declarations, var() with fallbacks, scoping and the cascade, runtime theming, and how they differ from Sass variables.
css-variables.q: How do CSS custom properties differ from Sass variables? Why are they powerful for theming?
css-variables.qsub: How would you implement a runtime dark-mode toggle using CSS variables?
css-variables.what:
Definition: CSS custom properties are declared as --name and used with var(--name). They are ordinary cascading properties, so you can change them at runtime through selectors, media queries, or JavaScript.

Sass variables are replaced at compile time, so they can't drive runtime theming.
css-variables.why: Dark mode, theme switching, and per-component customization (--card-padding) need no extra CSS. Change a variable with JavaScript and the whole subtree updates.
cons: var() can't be used inside media query conditions (for breakpoints)
gotchas: If a variable holds a value that is invalid for the property, the declaration fails at computed-value time. The fallback in var() applies only when the variable is undefined.
Names are case-sensitive: --Brand and --brand are different.
To animate a variable, register its type with @property.
terms: --brand: #0a84ff; is your own variable, changeable at runtime.
Read the value with var(--brand, fallback), optionally with a fallback.
The variable cascades and inherits, so overriding it on an element affects its children.
where: Put tokens on :root and override them on the theme.
Style knobs like --card-radius can be customized from outside the component.

flexbox.name: Flexbox — Main/Cross Axis
flexbox.desc: Flex container vs items, main and cross axis, justify-content, align-items, align-content, and flex-direction.
flexbox.q: Explain the flexbox axes. How do justify-content and align-items differ?
flexbox.qsub: How do you vertically and horizontally center a single element with flexbox?
flexbox.what:
Definition: Flexbox is a one-dimensional layout system (a row or a column) for aligning and spacing items. Apply display:flex to the container, and flex-direction sets the main axis.

justify-content works on the main axis, align-items on the cross axis, gap sets spacing between items, and flex-wrap lets items wrap onto a new line.
flexbox.analogy: Picture books on a shelf. The shelf runs in one direction (the main axis), and lining the books up by height is the cross axis.
flexbox.why: Navbars, toolbars, and card rows are far easier than with floats or inline-block. Equal heights, centering, and space-between all take a line or two.
cons: Grid is better for 2D layouts (rows and columns together)
gotchas: With flex-direction: column, the roles of justify and align swap.
Flex items default to min-width:auto, so long text can overflow. Set min-width:0.
align-content only works on multi-line (wrapped) containers
terms: The line of the flex direction (horizontal in a row). justify-content works along it.
Perpendicular to the main axis. align-items works along it.
The display:flex parent. Its direct children become flex items.
where: Responsive rows using gap and wrap.

flex-items.name: flex-grow / shrink / basis
flex-items.desc: The flex shorthand; how items share free space; flex-basis vs width; what flex:1 means.
flex-items.q: What does flex: 1 expand to and what does it actually do?
flex-items.qsub: What is the difference between flex-basis and width?
flex-items.what:
Definition: flex: grow shrink basis is a shorthand. flex: 1 means 1 1 0, an equal share. flex: none means no grow and no shrink. flex: 0 0 200px is a fixed 200 px.

First flex-basis sets the starting size. Then any leftover (or missing) space is divided according to the grow and shrink ratios.
flex-items.why: Keeping a sidebar fixed and letting the content take the remaining space (flex:1) is the most common flex pattern. Without understanding shrink, items can get squashed or overflow.
cons: The interaction between flex-basis and width can be confusing
gotchas: flex-basis overrides width (unless it is auto).
flex:1 has a basis of 0, so content size is ignored when sharing space.
If a long word or URL overflows, use min-width:0 or overflow-wrap.
terms: How much of the free space the item takes (as a ratio).
How much the item shrinks when space runs short.
The item's starting size before grow and shrink apply (takes priority over width).

grid-basics.name: CSS Grid — Tracks & Placement
grid-basics.desc: grid-template-columns/rows, the fr unit, repeat(), gap, minmax(), and auto-fit vs auto-fill.
grid-basics.q: When would you choose Grid over Flexbox? Explain fr and minmax().
grid-basics.qsub: What is the difference between auto-fit and auto-fill in repeat()?
grid-basics.what: Definition: CSS Grid is a two-dimensional layout system with rows and columns. Apply display:grid to the container and define tracks with grid-template-columns/rows. Items fill the cells automatically, and gap sets the spacing between tracks.
grid-basics.why: A responsive card grid takes a single line: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(220px, 1fr)). The number of columns adapts to the screen width without any media queries.
pros: 2D control, with easy alignment and spanning
cons: Flex is simpler for small 1D layouts
gotchas: fr tracks won't shrink below their min-content size. Use minmax(0,1fr) to prevent overflow.
The difference between auto-fit and auto-fill only shows when there are fewer items than tracks.
Implicit rows are controlled with grid-auto-rows.
terms: A fraction of the free space. 1fr 2fr gives a 1:2 ratio.
The minimum and maximum size of a track, for example minmax(200px, 1fr).
With repeat(), creates as many tracks as fit. auto-fit collapses the empty ones.
where: A 2D layout of sidebar, main, and header.

grid-areas.name: Grid Template Areas & Line Placement
grid-areas.desc: Named grid-template-areas, grid-column/row line placement, spanning, and implicit vs explicit grid.
grid-areas.q: How do grid-template-areas work? When are they clearer than line-based placement?
grid-areas.qsub: What is the implicit grid and how does grid-auto-flow affect it?
grid-areas.what:
Definition: grid-template-areas gives names to layout regions, and items opt in with grid-area: name. You can also place items by line number or span, such as grid-column: 1 / span 2.

The explicit grid is what the template defines. Extra items go into implicit tracks.
grid-areas.why: You can rearrange a page layout (header, sidebar, main, footer) inside a media query just by changing the template string, without touching the HTML order.
cons: When visual order differs from DOM order, keyboard navigation and screen readers can get confusing.
gotchas: Areas must be rectangular. L-shapes are not allowed.
Visual reordering does not change tab order (an accessibility concern).
A grid with n columns has n+1 lines, and line numbers start at 1.
terms: Names layout regions in an ASCII-art style that is easy to read.
grid-column: 1 / 3 places an item using line numbers.
Tracks you didn't define, which the grid creates because of the content.
where: Reordering header, nav, main, and footer.

positioning.name: Positioning — static/relative/absolute/fixed/sticky
positioning.desc: Normal flow vs positioned elements; containing block; offsets; sticky behaves like relative until a threshold, then like fixed.
positioning.q: Explain each position value. What is the containing block for an absolutely positioned element?
positioning.qsub: How does position: sticky decide when to stick, and why does it sometimes silently not work?
positioning.what: Definition: static is the default (normal flow). relative offsets the element from its original position while keeping its space reserved. absolute removes it from the flow and positions it against the nearest positioned ancestor. fixed positions it against the viewport. sticky sticks as you scroll.
positioning.why: Badges, tooltips, dropdowns, and sticky headers are all built with positioning. When an absolute element lands in the wrong place, it is usually because its parent doesn't have position: relative.
cons: Absolute elements are out of flow, so the parent's height collapses
gotchas: If an ancestor has overflow: hidden/auto, sticky stops working
An ancestor with transform becomes the containing block for fixed elements
sticky needs an offset such as top, or it never sticks
terms: The reference for an absolute element: its nearest positioned ancestor (relative, absolute, fixed, or sticky).
Behaves like relative until the scroll threshold is reached, then sticks like fixed.
where: A relative parent with an absolute child.
codeSwap: /* sticks to the top on scroll */

stacking-context.name: z-index & Stacking Contexts
stacking-context.desc: What creates a stacking context (position + z-index, opacity, transform) and why z-index:9999 can fail.
stacking-context.q: Why can a z-index: 9999 element still appear behind another? Explain stacking contexts.
stacking-context.qsub: Name three properties (other than z-index) that create a new stacking context.
stacking-context.what:
Definition: A new stacking context is created by the root element, position with a non-auto z-index, opacity < 1, transform, filter, isolation:isolate, and several other properties.

Elements in different contexts are ordered by their parent contexts' z-index, not by their own.
stacking-context.why: z-index: 9999 fails when your element sits inside a parent that belongs to a lower stacking context. The fix is to understand stacking contexts. Raising the z-index alone won't help.
pros: Components can manage their own z-index internally
cons: Hidden contexts (transform, opacity) are hard to debug
gotchas: opacity:0.99 or transform also creates a stacking context
z-index doesn't work on static elements (it does work on flex/grid items)
Don't render a modal deep inside the DOM. Use a portal
terms: An isolated group of layers. The z-index of its children only matters inside it.
The layer order of positioned, flex, and grid items. It is compared only within its own stacking context.
isolation: isolate creates a new stacking context without side effects.
where: Render the modal as a direct child of body via a portal to avoid context problems.

centering.name: Centering Techniques
centering.desc: Flex and grid centering, margin auto, absolute + transform, and when each applies.
centering.q: Give me three ways to center a box both horizontally and vertically. Trade-offs of each?
centering.qsub: How do you center an element of unknown width and height?
centering.what: Definition: The right technique depends on context. For text, use text-align:center. For a fixed-width block, use margin-inline:auto. For both axes, use flex or grid. For overlays, use position:absolute with inset:0; margin:auto (the element needs a set size).
centering.why: This is one of the most common interview questions. The modern answer is display:grid; place-items:center. Older methods (absolute with negative margins, table-cell) mostly appear in legacy code.
cons: Context-dependent: no single method works everywhere
gotchas: Give the parent a height (for example min-height), or vertical centering won't be visible
margin:auto needs a width on the block for horizontal centering
The absolute + transform method can make text look blurry
terms: Centers a block horizontally once its width is set.

float-legacy.name: Float & Clear (legacy)
float-legacy.desc: Historical layout with floats, the clearfix hack, and why floats caused collapsing parents.
float-legacy.q: What were floats originally for and why did they get abused for layout?
float-legacy.qsub: What is a clearfix and why was it needed?
float-legacy.what:
Definition: float was originally meant to wrap text around an image. In the 2000s it was repurposed for page layout (columns), which required clear and clearfix hacks.

Today flex and grid handle layout, and float is left for wrapping text around images.
float-legacy.why: You need this for reading legacy code and for interview questions. Floats are taken out of the flow, so the parent's height can drop to zero. This is called a “collapsing parent”.
pros: Still the right tool for wrapping text around an element
cons: Fragile and hacky for layout
gotchas: The parent collapses when its children are floated
clear only works against floats
Don't use float for new layouts. Use flex or grid
terms: Moves the element to the left or right so text wraps around it.
A hack that makes the parent stretch to contain its floated children.

container-queries.name: Container Queries
container-queries.desc: @container queries size components by their container instead of the viewport: true component-level responsiveness.
container-queries.q: How do container queries differ from media queries? Why are they a big deal for design systems?
container-queries.qsub: What is a containment context and how do you set one up?
container-queries.what: Definition: Media queries look at the viewport, while container queries look at the component's own parent. Set container-type: inline-size on the parent and write @container rules for the children.
container-queries.why: The same card component might appear in a narrow sidebar and in a wide main area. Media queries see the same viewport in both places, but container queries see the different container widths. That is what makes components truly reusable.
pros: Less dependence on global media query breakpoints
cons: container-type applies containment: with inline-size the width can't depend on the content, and with size the height can collapse
gotchas: A container can't restyle itself with its own query. Only its descendants can
With inline-size containment, the width is not determined by the content
Plan fallbacks for older browsers
terms: @container (min-width: 400px) changes the component's style based on its container's width.
Container query units, where 1cqw is 1% of the container's width.
where: A card or media object adapts to any context.
A widget's width changes as it moves within the grid.

media-queries.name: Media Queries
media-queries.desc: min-width and max-width breakpoints, feature queries, orientation, prefers-color-scheme, and prefers-reduced-motion.
media-queries.q: How do media queries work? What does prefers-reduced-motion let you do?
media-queries.qsub: What is the difference between min-width and max-width breakpoint strategies?
media-queries.what:
Definition: @media is conditional CSS. It applies rules based on viewport width (min-width/max-width), orientation, and user preferences such as dark mode, reduced motion, and contrast.

Mobile-first CSS typically builds up from the base styles with min-width.
media-queries.why: Media queries are the foundation of responsive design. User-preference queries (reduced motion, dark mode) matter for accessibility and polish. They go well beyond screen size.
cons: They are viewport-based, not component-based (container queries solve that)
gotchas: Set breakpoints where the content breaks, not at device names
Mixing max-width and min-width can cause overlaps or gaps
Hover-only interactions don't work on touch devices. Guard them with (hover: hover)
terms: The viewport width at which the layout changes. Let the content decide, not the device.
A browser support check. It is a feature query, not a media query.
where: The number of columns follows the viewport.
Reduced motion, dark mode, and high contrast.

mobile-first.name: Mobile-First Strategy
mobile-first.desc: Write base styles for small screens, then layer up with min-width. Why this approach produces simpler, faster CSS.
mobile-first.q: What does mobile-first mean in practice, and why is it preferred over desktop-first?
mobile-first.qsub: How does mobile-first reduce the number of CSS overrides?
mobile-first.what: Definition: Write the layout for the smallest screen first as plain CSS with no media queries, then add complexity with @media (min-width) as space becomes available.
mobile-first.why: Mobile devices parse less CSS and deal with fewer overrides. A single-column base layout is the natural starting point, and expanding it on larger screens is easier than tearing down a desktop layout to fit a phone.
cons: Migrating an existing desktop-first codebase takes real effort
gotchas: Mobile-first means using min-width, not max-width
Don’t forget touch targets (at least 44 px) and the viewport meta tag
Keep desktop assumptions (hover, fixed widths) out of the base styles
terms: Base CSS targets the small screen; larger screens are layered on with min-width.
A basic experience for everyone, with richer features for capable devices.
Base CSS targets large screens and smaller ones are overridden with max-width, which means more overrides.

fluid-typography.name: Fluid Type & clamp()
fluid-typography.desc: Use clamp(min, preferred, max) for fluid font sizes and spacing without breakpoints.
fluid-typography.q: How does clamp() work? Write a fluid font-size that scales between 16px and 24px.
fluid-typography.qsub: Why is clamp() often better than a stack of media queries for typography?
fluid-typography.what: Definition: clamp(1rem, 0.8rem + 1vw, 1.5rem) scales the font smoothly with the viewport, but never goes below 1rem or above 1.5rem.
fluid-typography.why: Instead of type that jumps at breakpoints, you get smooth scaling from a single line and fewer media queries. The same technique works for spacing.
cons: The values are a bit tricky to calculate (tools help)
gotchas: Using only vw breaks user zoom, so mix rem + vw
If min is greater than max, the min value wins
A very large max can ruin the line length
terms: Keeps the value between min and max while val grows with the viewport.
Font sizes and spacing scale continuously, with no jumps at breakpoints.
Sizing fonts with vw alone breaks zoom, so mix it with rem.

responsive-images.name: Responsive Images (srcset / sizes)
responsive-images.desc: Serve right-sized images per viewport and DPR with srcset and sizes, use <picture> for art direction, and reserve space with aspect-ratio.</picture>
responsive-images.q: How do you avoid shipping a 2000px image to a phone? Explain srcset + sizes.
responsive-images.qsub: How does the aspect-ratio property help prevent layout shift for images?
responsive-images.what: Definition: srcset + sizes lets the browser choose the best image for the viewport and DPR. <picture> provides a different crop or format. CSS max-width:100%; height:auto and aspect-ratio keep the image fluid.
responsive-images.why: A correctly sized image improves both LCP and data usage. If sizes is wrong, the browser picks an image that is too large, which is the most common mistake.
cons: You must generate and host multiple image variants (impractical without a CDN or build tool)
gotchas: Write sizes from the image’s layout width, not the viewport width.
Omitting width/height or aspect-ratio causes CLS.
object-fit crops the image; it does not stretch it.
terms: The actual width of each candidate: img-800.jpg 800w.
Tells the browser how wide the image will be in the layout so it can pick the right candidate.
Reserves space before the image loads with aspect-ratio: 16/9 (prevents CLS).
where: A tighter crop on mobile using <picture>.

viewport-units.name: Viewport Units & Mobile Gotchas
viewport-units.desc: vw, vh, vmin and vmax; the mobile 100vh address-bar problem; the dvh, svh and lvh dynamic units.
viewport-units.q: Why does 100vh behave badly on mobile browsers, and how do dvh/svh fix it?
viewport-units.qsub: When would you use vmin or vmax?
viewport-units.what:
Definition: vw/vh are viewport-relative units. On mobile the address bar hides and shows as you scroll, so 100vh assumes the larger viewport and content can end up hidden under the bar.

The fix: dvh (dynamic, follows the bar), svh (small, always safe), and lvh (large, as if the bar were hidden).
viewport-units.why: This is what causes the “cut off at the bottom” bug in full-screen hero sections and bottom-fixed buttons on mobile. The modern fix is dvh.
cons: With dvh, the layout can resize as the address bar moves during scroll
gotchas: 100vw includes the vertical scrollbar, so horizontal scroll may appear.
dvh can cause jitter during animation or resize; svh is safer.
Write a vh fallback first for older browsers.
terms: 1% of the viewport height or width.
Small, large and dynamic viewport height, defined by the state of the mobile address bar.
1% of the smaller or larger viewport dimension.
where: Use svh to stay within the safe area.

typography.name: Typography Control
typography.desc: The font shorthand, line-height, letter-spacing, font stacks and fallbacks, web-safe fonts, and text-wrap: balance.
typography.q: What makes body text readable? Talk about line-height, measure, and font fallbacks.
typography.qsub: What does a good font-family fallback stack look like, and why?
typography.what: Definition: These are the levers for readable typography: the font-family stack, font-size, line-height (about 1.5 for body text), letter-spacing, max-width in ch (45–75 characters), and text-wrap (balance for headings, pretty for paragraphs).
typography.why: Most of a UI is text, so typography has an outsized effect. Tight line-height, very long lines, or poorly matched fallback fonts hurt both readability and CLS.
cons: Custom fonts introduce a layout-shift trade-off (manage it with font-display)
gotchas: Keep line-height: 1.5 unitless, because inherited pixel or em values can give wrong results.
The font shorthand requires both font-size and font-family.
Input text smaller than 16px can trigger auto-zoom on mobile.
terms: A fallback list: font-family: Inter, system-ui, sans-serif.
A unitless value (1.5) is best because it scales with font-size.
Evens out the line lengths of a heading (reduces orphaned words).
where: max-width in ch plus a comfortable line-height.

overflow-ellipsis.name: Overflow & Text Truncation
overflow-ellipsis.desc: overflow: visible, hidden, scroll and auto; single-line ellipsis; multi-line line-clamp.
overflow-ellipsis.q: How do you truncate a single line of text with an ellipsis? What about multiple lines?
overflow-ellipsis.qsub: Why does text-overflow: ellipsis also require white-space and overflow to be set?
overflow-ellipsis.what: Definition: A single-line ellipsis needs three properties together: white-space: nowrap; overflow: hidden; text-overflow: ellipsis. For multiple lines, use line-clamp.
overflow-ellipsis.why: Long titles in cards and lists break layouts, and proper truncation is a common machine-coding and interview question. Flex children also need min-width:0.
cons: Content is hidden, so you need a tooltip or expand control to show the full text
gotchas: Flex items need min-width: 0 for the ellipsis to work.
text-overflow only takes effect when overflow is not visible (for example, hidden).
overflow: hidden can clip sticky positioning or box-shadow.

pseudo-classes.name: Pseudo-classes (:hover, :focus, :nth-child)
pseudo-classes.desc: State selectors, structural pseudo-classes, :focus-visible vs :focus, :not(), and functional pseudo-classes.
pseudo-classes.q: What is the difference between :focus and :focus-visible? Why does it matter for accessibility?
pseudo-classes.qsub: How would you style every third item in a list?
pseudo-classes.what: Definition: Pseudo-classes select an element by its state or position: :hover, :focus-visible, :checked, :disabled, :nth-child(), :not(), :has().
pseudo-classes.why: You can style states without any JS. :focus-visible is essential for accessibility (never remove the outline), and :has() enables parent-based rules such as “if this card contains an image, use a different layout”.
cons: Long chains of pseudo-classes increase specificity
gotchas: :focus also applies on mouse click, while :focus-visible applies during keyboard navigation
:nth-child counts all siblings, not just those of the same type (:nth-of-type behaves differently)
Hover-only UI does not work on touch devices
terms: Shows the focus ring only for keyboard navigation, not on mouse click.
Excludes elements; :has() works like a parent selector.

pseudo-elements.name: Pseudo-elements (::before / ::after)
pseudo-elements.desc: Generated content, the content property, decorative shapes, icons, and layout tricks.
pseudo-elements.q: What is the difference between a pseudo-class and a pseudo-element?
pseudo-elements.qsub: Give a practical use of ::before or ::after that you have actually used.
pseudo-elements.what: Definition: ::before/::after create a virtual child before or after an element's content. They require a content value (use "" for empty). Common uses are decorative icons, underline effects, clearfix, and overlays.
pseudo-elements.why: You get decoration without extra HTML elements. But don't put meaningful content (text users need to read) in a pseudo-element, because screen reader support and copy-paste behavior are unreliable.
cons: They can't be selected or manipulated from JS, and accessibility support is limited
gotchas: Without content, ::before does not render
Pseudo-elements don't work on replaced elements (img, input)
Don't put important text in a pseudo-element
terms: Generated content inside the element; the content property is required.
Style input placeholders and selected text.
An empty string creates a box for a decorative shape.
where: A gradient or dimming layer on top of a card.

backgrounds-gradients.name: Backgrounds & Gradients
backgrounds-gradients.desc: The background shorthand, multiple backgrounds, linear/radial/conic gradients, and background-size/position.
backgrounds-gradients.q: How do you layer multiple backgrounds? What is the difference between cover and contain?
backgrounds-gradients.qsub: How would you create a subtle striped background with a single gradient?
backgrounds-gradients.what: Definition: The background shorthand covers color, image, position, size and repeat. Gradients are background-image values. Multiple backgrounds stack with the first one on top.
backgrounds-gradients.why: Gradients and multiple backgrounds create rich visuals without image files, which keeps assets small and fast. Combining a gradient with an image is a common way to make overlaid text readable.
pros: Small, scalable, and no extra requests
cons: Complex gradients are hard to write and debug
gotchas: Background images have no alt text, so use <img> for meaningful images
In the shorthand, size follows the position, separated by /
Gradients can't be transitioned directly (use @property or an opacity trick)
terms: cover (fills the area, may crop) vs contain (fits entirely).
Gradients generated by CSS instead of image files.
Layers separated by commas: background: url(a), linear-gradient(...).
where: Image plus a dark gradient for text contrast.

shadows-radius.name: Borders, Radius & Shadows
shadows-radius.desc: border-radius, box-shadow (inset, spread), the drop-shadow filter vs box-shadow, and outline vs border.
shadows-radius.q: What is the difference between box-shadow and filter: drop-shadow? When does each matter?
shadows-radius.qsub: Why should you never remove focus outlines without providing an alternative?
shadows-radius.what: Definition: border-radius rounds corners (50% makes a circle). box-shadow draws a shadow behind the element's box, and multiple shadows are comma-separated. outline is like a border but does not affect layout.
shadows-radius.why: Shadows convey elevation (cards, modals), and layered soft shadows give more natural depth than flat styling. Use outline for focus indicators, and never use outline:none on its own.
cons: Large-blur shadows can be expensive to paint when animated
gotchas: box-shadow follows the element's box, not the shape of a transparent PNG (use drop-shadow for that)
Animating shadows triggers repaints; animating the opacity of an ::after is better
outline: none without a replacement is an accessibility bug
terms: x y blur spread color; add inset for an inner shadow.
A shadow that follows the element's actual shape (transparent PNG or SVG).
Outline takes no layout space and is meant for focus rings.

transitions.name: CSS Transitions
transitions.desc: transition-property, duration, timing-function and delay; which properties are animatable; easing curves.
transitions.q: How does a CSS transition work? Which properties are cheap to animate and which are expensive?
transitions.qsub: Why can transition: all be a performance foot-gun?
transitions.what: Definition: When a property's value changes, a transition automatically generates the intermediate frames between the two states. It runs when a state change is triggered (hover, class toggle). Syntax: property duration timing-function delay.
transitions.why: Small UI feedback (hover, open/close) doesn't need JavaScript. Choosing the right property is essential: transform/opacity stay smooth, while width/height trigger layout.
cons: Only works between two states; use keyframes for complex sequences
gotchas: transition: all can animate unexpected properties and hurt performance
display: none to block can't be transitioned (now possible with transition-behavior: allow-discrete or @starting-style)
You can't animate to auto height (use the grid-template-rows: 0fr to 1fr trick)
terms: Smoothly interpolates when a property’s value changes: transition: opacity .2s ease.
A property with continuous values (color, transform, opacity). display normally isn't one.

keyframes.name: Keyframe Animations
keyframes.desc: @keyframes, the animation shorthand, iteration, direction, fill-mode and play-state.
keyframes.q: How do @keyframes differ from transitions? When would you reach for each?
keyframes.what: Definition: @keyframes name { 0% {...} 100% {...} } defines a multi-step animation, which you apply with animation: name 1s ease-in-out infinite alternate. It can run on its own without a trigger.
keyframes.why: Loaders, attention pulses, entrance animations and similar sequences can't be built with transitions. Keyframes give you multi-step and looping animations in pure CSS.
pros: Multi-step and looping, with no JS
cons: Less control over dynamic values (JS data); the Web Animations API is better for that
gotchas: Without animation-fill-mode: both, the element snaps back to its un-animated state when the animation ends
Turn off infinite animations for users who prefer reduced motion
An animation and a transition on the same property can conflict
terms: Defines the animation steps with from/to or percentages.
forwards keeps the end state; backwards applies the start state during the delay.
How many times it runs: a number or infinite.

transforms.name: Transforms (translate / scale / rotate)
transforms.desc: 2D/3D transforms, transform-origin, why transforms don't trigger layout, and will-change.
transforms.q: Why is animating transform smoother than animating top/left?
transforms.qsub: What does transform-origin control, and when do you change it?
transforms.what: Definition: transform visually moves, scales, rotates or skews an element without changing layout (its original space stays reserved). Order matters: translate() rotate() and rotate() translate() produce different results.
transforms.why: Transforms skip layout and run on the compositor, so animations stay smooth (60fps). Animating left/top triggers layout, which is slow.
cons: Creates a new stacking context and containing block
gotchas: transform on an element becomes the containing block for its position:fixed descendants
It doesn't change the layout space, so elements can overlap
Don't apply will-change to everything; it consumes memory
terms: 2D transforms; individual properties now exist too: translate: 10px.
The point that rotate and scale happen around (the center by default).
Hints to the browser that a property will change, so it may promote the element to its own layer.

animation-perf.name: Animation Performance (compositor-friendly)
animation-perf.desc: Animate only transform and opacity to stay on the compositor, avoid layout and paint thrash, and keep a will-change budget.
animation-perf.q: Which two properties can you animate without triggering layout or paint, and why?
animation-perf.qsub: What does will-change do, and why should you use it sparingly?
animation-perf.what: Definition: For smooth animation, animate only transform and opacity. They skip layout and paint and run on the compositor, whereas width/height/top/left trigger layout and background/box-shadow trigger paint.
animation-perf.why: 60fps means 16ms per frame. Layout and paint run on the main thread and compete with JavaScript, while compositor animations stay smooth even when JS is busy. The DevTools Performance panel shows this clearly.
cons: Layout-based animations (such as height: auto) need a workaround
gotchas: Don't leave will-change applied permanently
To animate a shadow, animate the opacity of an ::after instead
Respect reduced-motion preferences
terms: transform and opacity animate on the GPU without involving the main thread.
Animating width, top or box-shadow forces layout or paint on every frame.
Use it only where needed; too many layers consume memory.

critical-render-path.name: Critical Rendering Path
critical-render-path.desc: DOM + CSSOM, render tree, layout, paint and composite; render-blocking CSS and JS; how the browser paints.
critical-render-path.q: Walk me through how the browser turns HTML and CSS into pixels on screen.
critical-render-path.qsub: Why is CSS render-blocking, and how do you reduce that cost?
critical-render-path.what: Definition: The browser builds the DOM from HTML and the CSSOM from CSS, combines them into a render tree, then runs layout (positions and sizes), paint (pixels) and composite (layers). CSS is render-blocking; synchronous JS blocks the parser and also waits on the CSSOM.
critical-render-path.why: First paint happens once the render tree is ready. Inlining critical CSS, deferring or lazy-loading the rest, and using defer on scripts improve FCP and LCP.
pros: Optimization can be targeted once you understand the rendering pipeline
cons: Maintaining critical CSS requires extra tooling
gotchas: A synchronous script pauses until the CSS download completes
@import creates a CSS request waterfall
Large CSS files block the entire page
terms: DOM and CSSOM combined; contains only visible nodes.
CSS (and synchronous JS) delay the page's first paint.
Compute geometry, fill in pixels, then combine layers on the GPU.
where: Inline critical CSS for a fast FCP.
Find blocking resources with Lighthouse or DevTools.

reflow-repaint.name: Reflow vs Repaint vs Composite
reflow-repaint.desc: Layout (reflow) recalculates geometry, paint fills pixels, and composite blends layers on the GPU. Which properties trigger which.
reflow-repaint.q: What is the difference between reflow, repaint, and composite? Which is the most expensive?
reflow-repaint.qsub: Give three property changes that force a reflow and three that only repaint.
reflow-repaint.what:
Definition: When a property changes, the browser does some combination of work: layout (width, margin, font-size, top) then paint then composite. Paint-only: color, background, box-shadow. Composite-only: transform, opacity.

If layout is triggered, paint and composite follow as well.
reflow-repaint.why: The fewer stages a change triggers, the cheaper it is. That's why animations use transform/opacity and why you shouldn't interleave DOM reads and writes.
pros: Understanding the pipeline is the foundation of rendering optimization
cons: You need to remember which properties trigger what (csstriggers-style references help)
gotchas: A small layout change can affect an entire subtree
display:none removes the element from layout, while visibility:hidden keeps its space
Reading layout properties in JS (such as offsetHeight) can force a reflow
terms: Refills pixels when color or shadow changes but geometry doesn't.
Combines layers on the GPU; the cheapest stage.
where: Inspect Layout and Paint events in DevTools.

layout-thrash.name: Layout Thrashing & Batching
layout-thrash.desc: Forced synchronous layout from read-after-write in JS, batching reads before writes, and requestAnimationFrame.
layout-thrash.q: What is layout thrashing? How do you avoid forced synchronous layout in a loop?
layout-thrash.qsub: Which DOM reads force a synchronous layout flush?
layout-thrash.what: Definition: Layout thrashing happens when a loop alternates reads (offsetHeight) and writes (style.height = ...), so each read forces the browser to recompute layout.
layout-thrash.why: In a loop over 100 elements that means 100 layouts; if you batch the reads first, it's just 1. This is the most common cause of jank when animating or measuring with JS.
pros: A big speedup from a small code change
cons: The code structure becomes slightly more rigid
gotchas: getBoundingClientRect, scrollTop and offsetHeight can all trigger forced layout
Prefer ResizeObserver/IntersectionObserver over polling layout values
Avoid mixing reads and writes inside effects, even in frameworks
terms: Reading a layout property right after changing styles forces the browser to run layout immediately.
Do all the reads first, then all the writes.
Schedules visual updates just before the next frame.

// thrash: read + write in every iteration

web-vitals.name: Core Web Vitals (LCP / CLS / INP)
web-vitals.desc: Largest Contentful Paint, Cumulative Layout Shift and Interaction to Next Paint: targets and common fixes.
web-vitals.q: What are the Core Web Vitals, and what causes a poor score in each?
web-vitals.qsub: How would you diagnose and fix a high CLS on a page?
web-vitals.what:
Definition: Core Web Vitals are three real-user experience metrics: LCP (loading), CLS (visual stability) and INP (responsiveness; it replaced FID).

Fixes: preload and optimize the LCP image, provide width/height and a matched fallback font to fix CLS, and break up long tasks to improve INP.
web-vitals.why: They are also Google search ranking signals and are directly tied to conversion. Lab data (Lighthouse) and field data (CrUX) can differ, and what counts is the field data from real users.
cons: Collecting field data (RUM) takes separate effort
gotchas: Don't lazy-load the LCP image
Late-loading ads, banners and fonts increase CLS
A good lab score can hide a poor field INP
terms: Largest Contentful Paint: when the largest content element is shown (target ≤ 2.5 s).
Cumulative Layout Shift: how much the layout moves around (target ≤ 0.1).
Interaction to Next Paint: how quickly the screen updates after a click or tap (target ≤ 200 ms).
where: Optimize the LCP image and CLS where conversions are sensitive.

font-loading.name: Web Font Loading (FOUT / FOIT)
font-loading.desc: font-display swap and optional, preloading fonts, fallback metrics, and layout shift from font swaps.
font-loading.q: What is the difference between FOUT and FOIT? How does font-display control it?
font-loading.qsub: How do you prevent a layout shift when a web font finishes loading?
font-loading.what: Definition: Until a web font finishes loading, the browser either hides the text (FOIT) or shows it in a fallback font (FOUT). font-display: swap shows the fallback immediately and swaps when the font arrives; optional uses the font only if it is already available (for example, cached), so there is no shift.
font-loading.why: A font swap changes text width and causes layout shift (CLS). Preloading plus a size-adjusted fallback (size-adjust, ascent-override) reduces the shift.
pros: Text appears quickly and shift is reduced
cons: Deriving accurate fallback metrics takes some work
gotchas: The crossorigin attribute is required on a font preload, otherwise the font may be downloaded twice
Don’t load too many weights or variants
Variable fonts reduce file size
terms: Flash of Unstyled Text: the fallback font appears first, then swaps.
Flash of Invisible Text: the text is hidden until the font arrives.

css-containment.name: CSS Containment & content-visibility
css-containment.desc: The contain property, content-visibility: auto to skip offscreen rendering, and performance isolation.
css-containment.q: What does content-visibility: auto do for a long page?
css-containment.qsub: What kinds of containment does the contain property offer?
css-containment.what: Definition: The contain property tells the browser that changes inside an element won't affect layout or paint outside it, so it can isolate the work. content-visibility: auto skips layout and paint for off-screen sections.
css-containment.why: On long pages (feeds, articles) it can dramatically cut initial render time. Without contain-intrinsic-size, skipped content has zero height, which makes the scrollbar jump.
pros: Lower initial render and scroll cost
cons: An incorrect intrinsic size causes scrollbar jumps
gotchas: contain: size stops the element’s size from being derived from its content, so provide an explicit size
Content skipped by content-visibility is still searchable with find-in-page and stays in the accessibility tree
Measure before applying it everywhere
terms: Tells the browser that changes in the subtree don't affect the outside: layout, paint, size, style.
Skips rendering of off-screen content and renders it as it scrolls into view.
A placeholder size for skipped content (prevents scrollbar jumps).

naming-bem.name: Naming Methodologies (BEM)
naming-bem.desc: BEM (block__element--modifier), and why naming conventions fight specificity and scale in large codebases.
naming-bem.q: What problem does BEM solve? How does it keep specificity flat?
naming-bem.qsub: What are the trade-offs of BEM versus utility-first CSS?
naming-bem.what: Definition: BEM (Block__Element--Modifier) is a naming convention: .block__element--modifier. The class name itself shows which component a style belongs to.
naming-bem.why: Global CSS suffers from name collisions and specificity wars. BEM uses flat, single-class selectors that all have the same specificity, which makes overrides predictable. The drawback is long class names.
cons: Verbose class names
Deep nesting makes names very long
gotchas: Don’t create chains like .card__title__link; flatten them
A modifier is never used alone; it is applied alongside the base class (card card--featured)
BEM is often unnecessary when you use scoped CSS (modules)
terms: A part of the block: .card__title (double underscore).

css-modules.name: CSS Modules & Scoping
css-modules.desc: Locally scoped class names, hashing, composition, and solving the global namespace problem.
css-modules.q: How do CSS Modules prevent class-name collisions? What does the build step do?
css-modules.qsub: How does composes work in CSS Modules?
css-modules.what: Definition: When a *.module.css file is imported, each class name is turned into a unique generated name (card_3xK9a), so collisions are impossible. You use them via styles.card.
css-modules.why: The global namespace problem is solved with no runtime cost (it's a static CSS file), and you keep everything plain CSS offers: media queries, pseudo-classes and tooling. For dynamic values, use CSS variables.
cons: Dynamic (props-based) styling needs CSS variables or inline styles
Naming conventions are still needed (for example, state classes)
gotchas: Global selectors (body, [data-theme]) need :global
Class names can't be built from dynamic strings with dot access; use bracket lookup like styles['x']
Overriding a child component’s styles is difficult (use CSS variables)
terms: Class names are local to the file; the build tool generates a unique hash.
Reuses another class’s styles inside a class.
Use :global(.x) when you need a global class.

css-in-js.name: CSS-in-JS (styled-components / emotion)
css-in-js.desc: Runtime vs zero-runtime CSS-in-JS, dynamic styling from props, SSR concerns, and performance trade-offs.
css-in-js.q: What are the pros and cons of CSS-in-JS? What is the runtime cost?
css-in-js.qsub: Why have zero-runtime solutions (Linaria, vanilla-extract) gained popularity?
css-in-js.what: Definition: CSS-in-JS writes styles in JavaScript alongside the component (using template literals or objects). Runtime libraries inject CSS during rendering, while zero-runtime tools extract static CSS at build time.
css-in-js.why: It offers colocation, dynamic styling and automatic scoping. The drawbacks are runtime overhead, SSR and streaming complexity, and friction with React Server Components, which is why the industry has moved toward zero-runtime tools, CSS Modules or Tailwind.
pros: Colocation, automatic scoping and dynamic styles
cons: Runtime cost and bundle size
Friction with RSC and streaming SSR
gotchas: Don't define styled() inside a component's render; every render creates a new class
SSR needs extra setup to prevent a flash of unstyled content (FOUC)
Make sure props don't leak to the DOM (use transient $prop)
terms: styled-components and emotion: styles live in JS and CSS is injected at runtime.
Linaria, vanilla-extract and Panda: static CSS is generated at build time.
Dynamic styles derived from component props.

utility-first.name: Utility-First CSS (Tailwind)
utility-first.desc: Utility classes, design tokens via config, purge/JIT, and when utility-first helps or hurts maintainability.
utility-first.q: What is the case for and against Tailwind / utility-first CSS?
utility-first.qsub: How does Tailwind keep the shipped CSS small?
utility-first.what: Definition: In utility-first CSS (Tailwind), you style HTML by applying small single-purpose classes instead of writing custom CSS. A config file (theme tokens) keeps spacing and colors consistent.
utility-first.why: There's no naming to agonize over, no dead CSS, and the design system is enforced. The drawbacks are long class strings and the discipline needed to extract components (reuse through React components, not @apply).
cons: Cluttered markup
The team has to learn the conventions
gotchas: Dynamic class names (bg-${color}-500) get purged, so write out full class names
Extract very long class lists into components
Overusing arbitrary values undermines design tokens
terms: Defined in the spacing and color config; utilities are generated from them.
CSS is generated only for the classes that are actually used.

theming-tokens.name: Design Tokens & Theming (dark mode)
theming-tokens.desc: Token layers, CSS variables for theming, prefers-color-scheme, and per-component theming without JS.
theming-tokens.q: How would you architect a themeable design system that supports light/dark and brand themes?
theming-tokens.qsub: Why are CSS variables better than duplicated stylesheets for theming?
theming-tokens.what: Definition: Keep tokens in two layers: primitive (--blue-600) and semantic (--color-primary: var(--blue-600)). Changing a theme means remapping the semantic tokens, and components use only semantic tokens.
theming-tokens.why: Dark mode, brand themes and high-contrast modes can all be handled by overriding CSS variables, with no JS rewrite. The color-scheme property also themes native controls (scrollbars, inputs).
pros: No JS rewrite and a runtime switch
cons: Requires discipline in token naming and governance
gotchas: To avoid a flash of the wrong theme, set the theme attribute before the page renders (inline script)
Check contrast ratios in both themes
Don't write raw hex values in components; use tokens
terms: A name based on purpose (--color-surface) rather than raw value (--gray-900).
The user's OS-level dark or light preference.

preprocessors.name: Preprocessors (Sass) & @layer
preprocessors.desc: Sass nesting, mixins and functions; native CSS nesting; and cascade layers (@layer) for predictable ordering.
preprocessors.q: What do preprocessors still offer now that CSS has variables and nesting?
preprocessors.qsub: What problem do CSS cascade layers (@layer) solve?
preprocessors.what:
Definition: Preprocessors like Sass added features CSS lacked (variables, nesting, mixins). Today CSS variables, nesting, @layer and color-mix() are native, so the need for a preprocessor has shrunk.

Using @layer reset, base, components, utilities; decides precedence by layer order instead of specificity.
preprocessors.why: Cascade layers give a structural fix for specificity wars: put third-party CSS in a lower layer and your styles in a higher one, and yours win without !important.
pros: Native nesting and variables keep the toolchain light
cons: Unlayered styles always beat layered styles, which can be confusing
gotchas: Layer order is set by the first declaration of each layer
Layer order is reversed for !important rules
Some things (mixins, functions) still have no native equivalent without Sass
terms: Variables, nesting, mixins and functions, compiled to CSS.
Cascade layers: a later-declared layer beats an earlier one, regardless of specificity.
where: Put the library in a lower layer.
